title: Make it: from a halide or an alkene to R-H and R-D
asks: A starting material and a product are given. List the steps and reagents.

know.h: The idea. An alkyl halide R-X is turned into an organometallic reagent R-M, and the reagent, a very strong base, is given a proton or a deuteron. Overall the halogen is replaced by H or by D.
Making a Grignard reagent. R-X + Mg in diethyl ether gives R-MgX. Write "Mg" over the arrow and "ether" under it.
Making an organolithium reagent. R-Br (or R-Cl) + 2 Li in pentane gives R-Li + LiBr. Two lithium atoms are needed for each halide. Either reagent does the job on this exam.
The last step chooses H or D. {{H2O}} gives R-H. {{D2O}} gives R-D. Nothing else changes.
Where the D goes. The D ends up on the carbon that carried the metal, and the metal sits on the carbon that carried the halogen. So the position of the halogen fixes the position of the D.
Starting from an alkene. First add HBr across the double bond to make the alkyl bromide. The Br goes on the more substituted carbon of the double bond: propene gives 2-bromopropane.

The homework. Propene to 2-deuteriopropane and to propane: (1) HBr gives 2-bromopropane; (2) Mg in ether, or 2 Li in pentane, gives the organometallic reagent; (3) {{D2O}} gives the product with D on the middle carbon, or {{H2O}} gives propane.

What an alkene cannot do. Because HBr puts Br on the more substituted carbon, the route from an alkene puts the D there too. To put D on the less substituted carbon, start from the halide that already has its halogen on that carbon.
One reagent per arrow, in order. Water or {{D2O}} is always its own, later step. Written together with the metal it would destroy the reagent as it formed. Number the steps: 1) Mg, ether; 2) {{D2O}}.

What must not be in the flask. The solvent and the halide must have no acidic hydrogen (no O-H, no N-H, no terminal alkyne C-H): the reagent has {{pKa}} 50 to 60 on its conjugate acid and takes any proton below that.
The reagent as a base on purpose. A terminal alkyne ({{pKa}} 25) gives its hydrogen to R-MgX. The alkyne carbon then carries the metal, and {{D2O}} puts a D there.
Skill. Work backwards from the product: find the D (or the new H), put a metal on that carbon, then a halogen, and only then ask which alkene, if any, gives that halide.

method: Compare the starting material with the product and find the carbon that gained the H or the D.
Work backwards: R-D comes from R-MgX or R-Li and {{D2O}}; the reagent comes from R-X with the halogen on that same carbon.
If the starting material is an alkene, add HBr first, and check that the Br lands on the carbon you need (the more substituted one).
Make the organometallic reagent: Mg in ether, or 2 Li in pentane.
Finish with {{D2O}} for D or {{H2O}} for H, as a separate step.
Write the route forwards, one arrow per step, with the reagent over the arrow and every intermediate drawn.

pitfalls.h: Writing Mg and water (or {{D2O}}) over the same arrow. The reagent must be made first, with no water present.
Using {{H2O}} when the product has a D, or {{D2O}} when it does not.
From an alkene, expecting the D on the less substituted carbon. HBr puts the Br, and so the D, on the more substituted one.
Going from the alkene straight to the organometallic reagent. The halide has to be made first.
Writing 1 Li. Two lithium atoms are needed: one ends up in R-Li, the other in LiBr.
Making the reagent in water or an alcohol instead of ether or pentane.
